caption:
Anthropic released Claude Opus 5 on 24 July 2026. It is priced at $5 per million input tokens and $25 per million output tokens, which is exactly what Opus 4.8 cost. Anthropic describes it as a model that comes close to the frontier intelligence of Claude Fable 5 at half the price.

On ARC AGI 3, an evaluation where the model has to solve novel problems, Anthropic reports Opus 5 scoring three times as high as the next best model. On one Frontier Bench task the model was given a drawing of a machine part and asked to write code to rebuild it, then intentionally given no way to view the drawing. It wrote its own computer vision pipeline to pull the geometry from the raw pixels and reconstructed the part. No competing model with the same setup solved it after five attempts.

The caveat is on slide 4, because it belongs there. Those Frontier Bench figures come from an internal run, mean reward over 5 attempts per task. Anthropic also says Opus 5 remains behind Mythos 5 on cybersecurity tasks.

Independent check: Simon Willison, writing on his own weblog, reports that Opus 5 is currently leading the Artificial Analysis leaderboard, in front of even Fable 5, and that it is priced the same as Opus 4.8.

Sources: anthropic.com/news/claude-opus-5 and simonwillison.net/2026/Jul/24/introducing-claude-opus-5/

Written with AI assistance. Every figure on these slides is quoted from the page it cites, and each quote is fetched and checked against the live page before anything is posted.

slides.title: They hid the drawing
slides.body: Opus 5 was handed a drawing of a machine part and told to write code that rebuilt it. Then it was given no way to look at the drawing. It **wrote its own code to read the picture**, pulled the shape out of the raw pixels, and rebuilt the part. No rival model managed it in five attempts.
slides.evidence: on one frontier-bench task, opus 5 was given a drawing of a machine part and asked to write code to rebuild it as a 3d freecad model. however, in this task, the model was intentionally given no way to directly view the drawing. opus 5 responded by writing its own computer vision pipeline to pull the geometry from the raw pixels, then reconstructed the full machine part. it succeeded in doing so repeatedly; no competing model with the same setup could solve it after five attempts.
